questions.stem: What is an outflow wind in a BC inlet?
options: Air flowing out of the mountains down the inlet to the water
Air flowing from the open water up into the inlet
A wind that blows from the south only, along the outer coast
A wind caused by fog draining off the land at night
questions.explanation: An inflow is air from the water into inlets; an outflow is air from the mountains toward the water.

questions.stem: Which outflow is typically very strong?
options: Summer afternoon inflow
Spring land breeze at dawn
Fog-driven drainage wind
Winter outflow from cold interior air
questions.explanation: Winter outflows are very strong; summer outflows at night can be strong and hazardous; summer inflows are usually not strong.

questions.stem: Outflows can make strong wind and rough water where?
options: Only far offshore, beyond the islands
At the head of every bay along the coast
At the inlet mouth, while nearby water stays calm
Only in the inner part of the inlet itself, near its head
questions.explanation: UBC notes outflows can create strong winds and rough seas at the mouth while nearby coastal waters remain calm.

questions.stem: In Howe Sound in summer, the Squamish wind outflow occurs overnight and early morning. What happens around noon?
options: It builds into a gale
It switches to an afternoon inflow
It dies away until the next night
It turns into a southeast land breeze
questions.explanation: The switch from morning outflow to afternoon inflow is described by UBC.

questions.stem: The Qualicum wind outflow into the Strait of Georgia runs about:
options: 16 to 20 knots, against 2 to 8 knots elsewhere
2 to 8 knots, the same as the rest of the strait
40 to 50 knots, gale force at the mouth
1 to 3 knots, lighter than the rest of the strait

questions.stem: Which conditions make a sea breeze?
options: A deep low and a gale over the coast
Cold land and warm water in winter
Heavy fog lying over the water
Sunny land well warmer than the water, high pressure, light wind
questions.explanation: A sea breeze is strongest from midday to mid-afternoon.

options: Cold air moving over warmer water
Rain evaporating on the land at night
Warm moist air cooled below its dew point over cooler water
Smoke from forest fires mixing with damp air
questions.explanation: Cold air over warm water makes sea smoke, which is short-lived and not a navigation hazard.

questions.stem: Which pair of statements about fog is correct?
options: Radiation fog forms at sea around noon; sea smoke is the main hazard
Radiation fog forms over land at night; sea smoke is not a hazard
Frontal fog is the same thing as sea smoke
Advection fog forms only in the winter months
questions.explanation: Advection fog is the main sea fog and can occur at any time of year.

options: Daytime warming, or wind mixing in drier air
Falling pressure as a low approaches the coast
A drop in temperature overnight
Calm wind and clear skies at night
questions.explanation: UBC lists sunlight warming the air and stronger wind mixing in drier air.

options: waves made by the wind blowing locally
waves made only by tidal races in passes
waves caused by fog banks moving offshore
waves from distant storms that travel far
questions.explanation: Local wind on swell makes a confused sea; a longer period means more energy.

questions.stem: Why does wind against a tidal current give worse seas?
options: It lowers the waves and smooths the sea
It calms the surface over the pass
The current shortens and steepens the waves into a chop
It raises the water temperature in the pass and so the waves
questions.explanation: The seas feel worse than the wind alone suggests.

questions.stem: A tide turns in a pass and the wind stays the same. What can happen?
options: Nothing changes until the wind itself changes
Waves can build quickly with no change in wind
The seas always flatten at the turn
The wind drops to calm at the turn
questions.explanation: A turning tide can build a flat windy channel into rolling waves.

questions.stem: Which is true of Sechelt (Skookumchuk) Rapids?
options: Flows can reach up to 17.6 knots
Flows never exceed 2 knots
They are safe at any stage of tide
They are in Haro Strait, near Victoria
questions.explanation: UBC gives up to 17.6 knots; some passes are navigable at slack but not at peak flow.
